hook: Temüjin united the feuding tribes of the Mongolian steppe, took the title Genghis Khan in 1206, and turned their horse archers against the rich settled lands around them.

sides.who: Mongol and Turkic steppe tribes united by Genghis Khan, later joined by conquered peoples and Chinese and Muslim siege engineers
Western Xia, Jin China, Qara Khitai, the Khwarazmian Empire, Georgia, the Rus' principalities, Poland, Hungary and the Abbasid caliphate
The Mamluk sultanate of Egypt and Syria, ruled by former slave-soldiers

resultLine: By 1260 the Mongols ruled from northern China to Russia and Iran, but on 3 September 1260 the Mamluks beat a reduced Mongol army at Ain Jalut and stopped their advance.

strategies.name: Speed, horses and the decimal army
strategies.text: Genghis organised his men in units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand. Each rider had several horses, so armies could cover huge distances fast and use feigned retreats to trap enemies.

strategies.name: Siege engineers and terror
strategies.text: The Mongols recruited Chinese and Muslim engineers to build catapults. Cities that resisted were massacred and the news spread on purpose, so many others surrendered without a fight.

strategies.name: The ambush at Ain Jalut
strategies.text: Hulagu had taken most of his army east, leaving one tumen under Kitbuqa. Baybars pretended to flee, drew the Mongols into the hills, and hidden Mamluk troops closed in.

impact: The sack of Baghdad in 1258 ended the Abbasid caliphate after about 500 years.
Civil war after 1260 split the empire into four khanates: the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate and Yuan China.
Under Mongol peace, merchants, envoys, goods, technologies and ideas moved more freely across Eurasia than ever before.

sources.title: Timothy May, 'The Chinggis Exchange: the Mongol Empire and Global Impact on Warfare', World History Connected
